title: Getting started and finding your way
summary: Build your first project and learn where tools and settings live.

sections.title: Projects, boards and items
paragraphs: A project contains boards, collaborators and a file library. A board is a large workspace you can pan and zoom. An item is one object on a board: a note, Kanban, image or another block.
The top bar contains projects, search, sharing, project tools and your account. Create items with the left sidebar. Selecting an item opens the editbar and inspector.

sections.title: Make your first board
steps: Choose a project in the top-left menu, or add a new one.
Expand a tool group. Select Sticky Note, then click the canvas, or drag the tool directly onto it.
Double-click the note text to edit. Finish by clicking outside the editor or using its completion action.
Select the note and change its appearance in the editbar. Add a tag in the inspector.
Check the save indicator before leaving. Changes save automatically.
sections.example: Create a “New website” project with a goal note, requirements checklist and Kanban. Add separate boards for research and delivery later.

sections.title: Finding help
paragraphs: User guide is at the bottom of Tools. A collapsed sidebar shows a book icon; on mobile, open Tools first. It is also available in your profile and administration.
Search this guide by tool or action. Click an illustration to enlarge it. Button explanations open on hover or keyboard focus.

sections.title: Demo versus a server connection
paragraphs: The demo stores data in this browser. Clearing site storage or using a different browser gives you a separate dataset. The library, sharing, collaboration and some account/administration actions require the API.
sections.tip: Your installation may use a custom name, logo and palette. These instructions describe the underlying functions regardless of branding.

image.alt: Workspace with tools, the canvas and the project bar
image.caption: Screenshots show real application components with fictional training data. Labels, colours and available actions depend on language, permissions and server configuration. The shared screenshots use the Polish interface.

title: Navigation and selection
summary: Move around the canvas, zoom into details and select items without accidentally editing.

sections.title: Moving the view
steps: Hold Space and drag to pan, or drag with the middle mouse button.
Use the mouse wheel over the canvas to zoom around the pointer. Zoom and fit-view controls are also available by the board.
On touch screens, pan and pinch. Tools, editing and details panels open as separate windows.
sections.tip: The wheel scrolls content inside a scrollable item. Over the canvas it zooms. Use Space or the middle button to pan over an item.

sections.title: Selecting and editing
paragraphs: Use Select & move and click an item to select it. Drag on empty canvas to draw a selection box. Shift extends selection.
Drag an item by its background or header. Inputs, buttons and handles perform their own actions. Many blocks enter editing on double-click; complex blocks also provide edit buttons.
Escape cancels the current operation or clears selection. Selection handles resize an item.

sections.title: Canvas shortcuts
paragraphs: Ctrl/Cmd+C copies selection, Ctrl/Cmd+V pastes, Ctrl/Cmd+D duplicates and Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes. Delete or Backspace removes selected items, with confirmation where required.
Canvas shortcuts leave normal typing in text inputs and editors alone. Editors may provide their own undo.
sections.example: Copy three notes, paste them into another part of the board and drag the set into place.

title: Editbar and item appearance
summary: Selection opens a compact toolbar with options relevant to the selected item types.

sections.title: Tabs and scope
paragraphs: The first available tab opens when you select an item. Appearance includes backgrounds, accents, borders and resetting styles. Text controls typography. Layout provides arrangement and sizing where supported.
Multiple selection shows shared options. Check the selection count before applying a colour, grouping or deleting.

sections.title: Style an item
steps: Select an item and open Appearance.
Choose a palette or custom colour. Depending on the block, adjust transparency, gradients, accent strips and borders.
In text settings, choose a font with a visual preview, size, weight, italic style and alignment. The larger font preview helps compare families.
Use the visible reset appearance button to remove item appearance overrides. It does not delete content.
sections.example: Use a shared accent for decision notes, larger headings for section titles and neutral colours for supporting material.

sections.title: Layers and tool-specific options
paragraphs: Bring to front/send to back changes stacking order. Groups help select and move a set together.
Arrows have endpoint, curve and label settings; columns have layout options; section titles have label styles. Controls depend on the current selection.
sections.tip: Item appearance and application appearance are separate. Find application settings under Project tools → Appearance.

image.caption: A selected note with the Appearance tab open. Tabs depend on the type and number of selected items.

title: Inspector, tags, statuses and comments
summary: The right panel describes selection and helps organise collaboration.

sections.title: Tags and search
steps: Select one or more items.
Add a tag in the inspector. Remove a tag using its label action.
Search from the top bar by content or #tag. The search also supports status:identifier.
sections.example: Tag notes #to-discuss and search that tag during a meeting to find scattered questions.

sections.title: Statuses and comments
paragraphs: Assign project statuses to items. The status manager organises names and styles; permissions determine the available actions.
Open an item’s comments to leave feedback or discuss it. Distinguish resolved and unresolved threads. Commenters can manage their own comments without editing the board.
Public project links do not publish comments. With multiple selection, check the operation’s scope in the panel.

sections.title: Item locks
paragraphs: Locking prevents movement and manual resizing and captures the current item height. Further content scrolls inside that height instead of growing the block. Content remains editable.
Hover, focus or click the lock badge for an explanation. A frame containing a locked item can inherit a movement restriction; its explanation distinguishes this from a direct lock.
Unlock to resize again. In blocks with auto-height, you can then enable fitting height to content.

image.caption: The selected item’s inspector with locking, tags and comments. On smaller screens, open the details panel.

title: Context menus and arrangement
summary: Reach common actions without looking through several panels.

sections.title: Right-click menus
paragraphs: Right-click empty canvas for board actions. Right-click an item or selection for actions such as copy, duplicate, layer ordering, locking, grouping and deleting.
On touch devices, use the canvas action menu and panel buttons instead of relying on a right mouse button.

sections.title: Automatic arrangement
steps: Select the items to organise.
Open Distribute evenly and choose the layout, gap and items per row or available width.
Review the preview. Fill gaps is enabled by default and tries to place smaller items in space below shorter neighbours.
Apply. Turn off Fill gaps for a more regular row-based arrangement.
sections.example: Two tall checklists and small notes leave uneven spaces. Fill gaps uses the space below shorter items.
sections.tip: Groups and locks affect arrangement availability. Read the dialog explanation if an operation is unavailable.

sections.title: Deleting and recovering
paragraphs: Deleted items go to item trash, available through board/project actions. Restore or permanently remove them there.
Project trash is separate, inside the project menu. Emptying trash and permanent deletion differ from undoing the latest edit.

image.caption: Canvas context menu. Commands depend on where you click, selection and permissions.

title: Notes, text, documents and code
summary: Choose a format suited to the type and length of content.

sections.title: Sticky notes and the dispenser
paragraphs: Notes hold short ideas, decisions and meeting content. Double-click to edit; select for colours, typography and height fitting.
Pull new notes from the note dispenser onto the canvas. Its settings help maintain a shared style. Generated notes edit and move like ordinary notes.
sections.example: Use a yellow “Ideas” dispenser in a brainstorming workshop, with one idea per note.

sections.title: Text and section titles
paragraphs: Text is useful for short captions and headings without a sticky-note background. Section titles divide areas and offer their own label and background styles.
Double-click to edit content and use the editbar for size, alignment and colours.
sections.example: Divide a board into “Problem”, “Ideas” and “Decisions”; put small text captions beside connections.

sections.title: Documents and code
paragraphs: Documents provide rich text for descriptions, headings and lists. Edit inside the block; choose auto-height or a fixed scrollable size for longer material.
Code blocks store snippets and use the selected language for syntax highlighting. They do not automatically execute your code.
Locking preserves height while editing documents and code too.
sections.example: Place a decision document and an API request snippet beside an architecture diagram.

image.caption: Notes, a document and a code block. Each has its own editor; selection controls appearance and movement.

title: Checklists and Kanban
summary: Plan work, assign people, set deadlines and filter tasks.

sections.title: Checklists and task details
paragraphs: Add a titled entry and mark completion with its checkbox. Checklists work well for procedures, acceptance criteria and simple lists.
Tasks can include a description, assignee, categories and deadline. Open the task’s details/edit action. Assignees come from project participants; title-only tasks can remain unassigned.
Only unfinished tasks changes visibility. Completed tasks remain in the data and return when the option is disabled.

sections.title: Columns and cards
steps: Add Kanban from Organize. Name it and prepare stages such as To do, In progress and Done.
Click a column title or icon to change its name, icon and appearance. Arrow buttons reorder columns; a separate button removes one.
Add tasks and drag cards by their handles. Completion and column position are separate pieces of information.
Use plus to add a column. Board width grows by the column module and gap. Resize a column with its handle.
sections.tip: Check column content before removing it. Use arrows when you only want to change column order.

sections.title: Filtering tasks
steps: Click Filter beside Only unfinished tasks.
Choose all assigned people or individual people. Include unassigned independently includes tasks without an assignee, including title-only cards.
Select one or more categories. A card may match any selected category, but person, category, text and deadline conditions must all match.
Optionally search title/description and set Deadline before. The selected day is excluded. A separate option includes tasks without a deadline.
Apply and check the result count. The filter button is highlighted when active. Reset filter clears conditions while preserving Only unfinished tasks.
sections.example: To find Anna’s overdue urgent work, enable unfinished-only, choose Anna, exclude unassigned, select Urgent and choose tomorrow to include deadlines through today.
sections.tip: Filters belong to the current Kanban view and do not change task data. Dragging filtered cards preserves hidden cards.

image.caption: Kanban with the filter dialog. Filters narrow the view without deleting tasks or restoring completed cards hidden by Only unfinished tasks.

title: Columns, frames and linked boards
summary: Give a large project a readable structure.

sections.title: Columns as containers
paragraphs: Columns organise nested items. Drag items in, reorder with handles and move them back to the canvas when needed.
Use layout controls in the editbar to arrange contents. Headers and backgrounds distinguish work areas.
sections.example: A “Meeting materials” column can contain an agenda document, preparation checklist and reference link.

sections.title: Frames and groups
paragraphs: Frames mark an area of the canvas. Give a frame a title and place related items inside for workshops or process stages.
Groups select and move a set together. Ungroup when you need to work on individual parts again.
A locked item inside a frame restricts frame movement. The lock explanation identifies inherited restrictions.

sections.title: Linked board cards
steps: Add Board and create or open a linked project board.
Give the card a name, description and icon explaining its destination.
Open the card to navigate. Use board navigation to return to earlier locations.
sections.example: A project home board can link to “Research”, “Release plan” and “Documentation” without splitting participants or the library.

title: Arrows, icons and drawing
summary: Explain relationships and add visual cues.

sections.title: Connect items
steps: Insert Line / Arrow and select it.
Drag one endpoint onto the first item’s edge. Highlighting indicates an attachment edge. Place the other endpoint on the second item.
Fixed attachment points are enabled by default, preserving the chosen position on each edge as items move.
Disable fixed attachment points in the editbar to let endpoints slide along their chosen edges. The attachment edges remain preserved.
Adjust arrowheads, colour, thickness, curve, label, label rotation and distance in the editbar.
sections.example: Connect the right edge of “Decision” to the left edge of “Delivery”. Fixed points retain those positions after moving the notes.

sections.title: Dividers and icons
paragraphs: A divider separates areas and snaps to the grid; it does not attach two items together.
Icon / Emoji supports presets, emoji and supported custom sources. Use a label to make meaning clear.
sections.example: Mark risks with warning icons and completed stages with check marks. Labels explain meaning without relying on colour.

sections.title: Pencil
paragraphs: Select Pencil and draw on the canvas. Escape returns to selection. Select a drawing to style it; smoothing reduces jitter and point count.
Use drawing for sketches and emphasis. Use attached arrows for relationships that should follow items.

image.caption: Connected notes and arrow settings. Highlighted edges help place endpoints correctly.

title: Timeline, mind maps and diagrams
summary: Planning blocks have dedicated editors inside their items.

sections.title: Timeline
paragraphs: Open the timeline editor, add tasks and set dates. Available views and settings adapt the level of detail to the plan.
Finish editing to move the whole block. Planning editor changes save with the project.
sections.example: Plan analysis, design, implementation and testing as release tasks, with a Kanban beside them for delivery.

sections.title: Mind map
paragraphs: Develop a central topic into branches. Edit node text and add connected topics. Layout and connection appearance can be adjusted.
Outside editing, the map is one item that can be moved, resized, tagged and locked.
sections.example: For “New product”, add “Audience”, “Problems”, “Solutions” and “Risks” branches.

sections.title: Diagrams and database diagrams
paragraphs: Use Diagram to add and connect nodes describing a system or process.
Use Database diagram to model tables, fields, types and relations. Add them in the block editor and arrange the layout for readable connections.
A database diagram is visual documentation; drawing a table does not create a real database table.
sections.example: Document a support process and separately model Tickets, Users and Comments tables.

image.caption: Planning tools on a board. The outer item size and its internal node layout are separate.

title: Images, files, links and embeds
summary: Combine external content with project material.

sections.title: Images and files
paragraphs: Image displays a graphic with size and caption options. Select a library asset or a supported source in the editor.
File represents an attachment such as a document or spreadsheet. Preview support depends on format; files can also be downloaded. Library selection preserves the project asset reference.
sections.example: Place a mockup image and requirements attachment beside acceptance criteria, and include their version in the caption.

sections.title: Link cards and Embed
paragraphs: Link cards store a URL with a title and description. Use them for references that do not need embedding.
Embed displays supported content, such as a video. Paste a URL in its editor. Some sites prevent embedding or require login; use an ordinary link in those cases.
Media controls interact with content; use the item header or background to move the block.

sections.title: Access to material
paragraphs: Material visible to you may require access to its source. Project sharing and publicly sharing an individual library asset are separate actions.
Test public project links in a signed-out window and verify the intended files are available while private material stays private.

title: Project library
summary: Keep assets together, find them quickly and control access.

sections.title: Upload and find files
steps: Open Project tools (three dots in the top bar) → Library.
Choose Upload files or drag files into the library. Accepted formats and limits depend on the server, and preview support varies.
Use search, type filters and sorting by name, date or size.
Select a file to inspect it. When choosing content for a block, use Use file to insert it.

sections.title: Names, previews and deletion
paragraphs: People with management access can rename or delete assets. Renaming differs from uploading a replacement file.
Check whether an asset is used before deleting it: existing blocks referencing it may lose access.
sections.example: Use names such as “Login screen mockup” and “Release 2 specification” rather than relying on original filenames.

sections.title: Private files and public links
paragraphs: Files are private by default. An authorised person can create and copy a public asset link. Anyone with that link can access the material.
Revoking the link removes access through it. Hiding a block does not revoke asset sharing.
sections.tip: Project JSON contains asset references, not the binary files. Preserve access and back up files separately.

image.caption: Project library with files and a details panel. The library requires the API; the illustration uses training materials.

title: Managing projects and boards
summary: Create, name, organise and recover workspaces.

sections.title: Project menu
steps: Open the project name in the top bar.
Add a named project and choose a colour.
Click a project to switch to it; use its rename action to update its name.
Set a default project if you want to start in that workspace.
Move an owned project to trash when needed. Restore or permanently delete it in the trash section.

sections.title: Multiple boards
paragraphs: Use board navigation and linked board cards to split a project into named spaces.
The app saves data and retains view state as you navigate. Browser history can return to visited locations.
sections.example: An “Event” project can have Plan, Speakers, Promotion and Event day boards while sharing participants and assets.

sections.title: Automatic saving and recovery
paragraphs: Check saving, saved and error states. If connectivity fails, read the available retry or local recovery actions.
Project tools → Refresh tries to save changes before reloading projects. Do not ignore save failures.
Trash helps recover accidental deletion but does not replace server and file backups.

image.caption: Project menu with projects and actions. Available operations depend on your role; shared projects appear in the same list.

title: Sharing and collaboration
summary: Match roles to responsibilities and publish only what is needed.

sections.title: Invite a collaborator
steps: As owner, open a project and click Share.
Enter the email of an existing account in this installation.
Choose Editor, Commenter or Viewer and confirm.
The project appears in their list. Owners can change roles or remove participants later.

sections.title: Roles
paragraphs: Owners manage membership, public links and the project lifecycle. Editors can change boards and items.
Commenters read the project and manage their own comments. Viewers have read access. Neither role gains item editing rights.
View filters differ from data changes. Live collaboration may show presence, selection and cursors; the top bar indicates connection status.
sections.example: Give delivery team members Editor, reviewers Commenter and report recipients Viewer.

sections.title: Public read-only links
steps: Create a public link in sharing settings, optionally with a label and expiry.
Copy it and test in a signed-out window.
Recipients can view without an account. Comments are not published.
Remove the link when no longer needed and separately review public library links.
sections.tip: Anyone possessing a valid public link can use it. Changing a participant role does not revoke a separately created link.

image.caption: Sharing dialog with participant roles and public links. Sharing needs a server-saved project; names shown are fictional.

title: Exporting and importing data
summary: Save a project’s structure as JSON and import it as a project.

sections.title: Export
steps: Open the project to export.
Choose Project tools → Export JSON.
Save the downloaded file, named from the project.
Preserve access to library assets: the file contains references, not their binary contents.

sections.title: Import
steps: Choose Project tools → Import JSON.
Select a supported project file. The UI limit is 20 MB; invalid structures are rejected.
Wait for import confirmation and automatic saving.
Check boards, links and assets. References from another installation do not upload their files automatically.
sections.example: Export before a major reorganisation, then import a comparison copy instead of recreating notes manually.

sections.title: Separate backups
paragraphs: Project exports do not contain accounts, passwords, server configuration, audit or library files. Operators need separate database and file-store backups.
A JSON file can contain confidential project content. Protect it as carefully as the project itself.

image.caption: Project tools with JSON transfer, appearance and library actions. JSON is not a full backup of the server or library.

title: Profile, password and account security
summary: Update personal details and protect sign-in.

sections.title: Details and profile photo
steps: Open Account menu → Profile and security.
Change your display name or email. Email changes require your current password.
Save and check confirmation.
Click the avatar to select and, where available, crop a supported image. Save or cancel its preview.

sections.title: Password and MFA
paragraphs: The password form asks for current, new and confirmation passwords. Use at least 12 characters with uppercase, lowercase, a number and a symbol. Other signed-in sessions close after changing it.
Configure available MFA methods, such as an authenticator or email, using the setup flow and confirmation code.
Store recovery codes safely outside the app. Security method changes may require renewed identity verification.
sections.tip: Administrator accounts may have additional MFA requirements. Use recovery procedures rather than sharing passwords or codes.

sections.title: Language, session and deletion
paragraphs: Change language and toggle light/dark mode in the account menu. Full appearance settings are in Project tools.
Signing out ends the session. Profile also contains the security data notice and account deletion section.
Read the deletion plan for owned projects; it may require deleting projects or transferring ownership. Review consequences before confirming.

image.caption: Profile with account details, password and security. Some actions require the API. No passwords or recovery codes are shown.

title: Application and canvas appearance
summary: Adjust themes, colours, fonts and the workspace.

sections.title: Interface settings
steps: Open Project tools → Appearance.
Choose the interface theme, palette and font and review the preview.
Adjust sidebar width. On desktop, drag its right edge; double-click the handle to reset width.
Save settings, or use the reset action when needed.

sections.title: Canvas and semantic colours
paragraphs: Canvas settings control the workspace appearance. Choose backgrounds and palettes that keep notes, lines and selection readable.
Items using palette roles can respond to theme changes. Custom fixed colours are separate overrides; check contrast on very dark or light backgrounds.
sections.example: Use a calm background for long sessions and a strong accent for active controls. Choose a few readable workshop colours to separate topics.

sections.title: Advanced styles
paragraphs: Some settings support custom item/status CSS. Make deliberate changes and verify editing, scrolling and readability.
For an unusually styled item, check its editbar overrides and use Reset appearance. Resetting application preferences is a different operation.
Changing the installation name and logo is an administrator action covered under Branding.

image.caption: Appearance settings for interface and canvas. These are separate from individual item styles.

title: Administration: users and projects
summary: Administrative actions require an Administrator account.

sections.title: Users
steps: Open Account menu → Manage users. Administrators may start directly in administration.
Search Users by name, email or ID and filter by status.
Create accounts or use available edit, role, block, password/appearance reset and recovery actions.
Check the target account and scope before confirming. Administrator privileges affect the whole installation.

sections.title: Projects and ownership
paragraphs: Search and filter projects by state and participants, manage membership and transfer ownership.
Recovery and permanent removal depend on project state. Permanent removal is different from moving to trash.
Transfer ownership to the correct account when project responsibility changes.
sections.example: When a team lead changes, find their projects, verify membership and transfer ownership rather than rebuilding data.

sections.title: Registration, email and MFA
paragraphs: Allow registration controls self-service account creation without deleting existing users.
Email settings cover delivery, templates and the outbox. Check these when confirmation, password reset or code messages do not arrive.
MFA resets have their own administrator verification requirements. Verify the requester’s identity before using recovery actions.

image.caption: Administration with fictional user accounts and status filters. Installation administrators and project owners are different roles.

title: Administration: audit and incidents
summary: Investigate events in context rather than relying on a single counter.

sections.title: Reviewing events
steps: Open Administration → Audit.
Use Events filters such as severity, type, user, time or outcome and apply them.
Inspect an event’s UTC time, outcome, route, request identifiers and related events.
Refresh as needed. Audit persistence failures can affect history completeness.

sections.title: Incidents
paragraphs: Use Incidents and review-status filters to find signals needing investigation.
Compare events with user activity and environment configuration. Update review status after investigating according to your team’s process.
An alert alone is not proof of intrusion, and no alert does not guarantee security. This panel shows events recorded by the application.
sections.example: For repeated failed sign-ins, check the user, IP, time range and subsequent outcomes before deciding on an account or IP block.

sections.title: Retention and operations
paragraphs: History follows server retention settings and is not an independent forensic backup of infrastructure activity.
Correlate app audit with reverse-proxy and database logs available to operators. Maintain deployment, retention and backup procedures outside the UI.

image.caption: Audit filters and statistics. Times are UTC and statistics cover the last 24 hours. The illustration contains no production data.

title: Administration: security monitoring
summary: Review IP addresses, blocks and account requirements within the panel’s scope.

sections.title: Addresses and blocks
paragraphs: Administration → Security provides IP views and available blocking actions. Inspect address details before changing access.
Choose Ban IP, enter one IPv4 or IPv6 address, a reason and duration or a permanent ban. Releasing a ban clears failure counters; subsequent abuse can trigger a new ban.
People behind one company network or proxy can share an IP; blocking it can affect all of them.

sections.title: Routine review
steps: Review open incidents and audit warnings.
Check blocked accounts, administrator roles and registration settings.
Check email delivery and privileged-account MFA requirements.
Review public links and project permissions if access is reported unexpectedly.
Outside the app, check updates, HTTPS, backups and correct reverse-proxy client-IP forwarding.
sections.tip: This panel is not a vulnerability scanner and does not replace infrastructure testing or deployment reviews.

sections.title: Suspected abuse
paragraphs: Record event identifiers and times, restrict access using the appropriate control and investigate related operations. Preserve information needed for investigation.
After review, update incident status and check that the restriction does not prevent authorised work.

image.caption: Administrative security and IP controls. Options depend on server configuration; this is not a scan of a real installation.

title: Administration: application name and logo
summary: Customise the identity of the entire installation.

sections.title: Name
steps: Open Administration → Branding.
Enter an application name and save it.
Check the header, browser tab title and sign-in page. Other users see this change.

sections.title: Logo
steps: Choose Change application logo.
Select a supported image and review it; adjust cropping if available.
Save. Cancelling leaves the current logo unchanged.
Check the header and browser tab icon. Use the remove-image action to return to the default mark.
sections.tip: Use a simple mark that remains readable at favicon size and on light and dark backgrounds.

sections.title: Shared identity versus personal preferences
paragraphs: Name and logo are installation-wide. Appearance preferences adjust the working interface, while item styles belong in the editbar.
Branding changes do not migrate projects or files or alter participant permissions.

image.caption: Application branding with name and logo controls. Branding is shared and includes the sign-in page.
